doc.title: Vi Redd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999

title: Starting out during and after World War II
summary: She was still in school during the war, her father kept her out of clubs, and she began playing sorority dances in 1948-49.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Is it okay if I reach over and get some coffee?
Yeah, sure, because we’re kind of informal here, so.
I have to start the question again.
During World War II, when a lot of the fellows were in the service, did that make a difference for the opportunities for women?

Well see I was still in school then. I didn’t really start until ’48, that’s when I got out of high school. But see I wasn’t playing then. My father wouldn’t let me come in the clubs, that was taboo. You know at that age. I got started really like in the early 50s, and the late — oh ’48, ’49 is when I got my little band together and I started playing all these sorority events and things like that. Sororities, fraternity dances, we used to play over at the place call the Alpha Bowling Club. It’s a church now. And I’d play one night and Hampton Hawes would have a band there the other night. And the war thing, when the war was going on, I was in school see? So I wasn’t out there trying to compete for jobs. My father was really active at that time. And he did well.
